summary.text: Thermohaline circulation is the part of the ocean's large-scale circulation driven by global differences in seawater density, which come from surface heat and freshwater fluxes.
Its name joins the words for temperature and salt, the two factors that together set how dense seawater is.
Its waters carry heat, dissolved solids and gases around the globe, so the state of the circulation greatly affects Earth's climate.

facts.label: Popular nickname
facts.value: Ocean conveyor belt, coined by Wallace Smith Broecker

facts.label: Oldest waters
facts.value: About 1000 years in transit, upwelling in the North Pacific

facts.label: Two main limbs
facts.value: AMOC in the North Atlantic, SMOC near Antarctica

facts.label: Collapse outlook
facts.value: Generally thought to be more than a century away

items.prompt: In the North Atlantic, evaporation leaves the surface water extra salty and chills it further. What does this water do next?

options.label: It rises and spreads as a thin warm layer
It sinks down toward the deep ocean
It freezes solid into a floating ice sheet
It flows straight into the Pacific Ocean

items.explain: Salty, cold water is dense, so it sinks in the Norwegian Sea and then spills southward.

items.prompt: Fresh lake water is heaviest at 4 °C. How does seawater behave as it is cooled toward its freezing point?

options.label: It is also heaviest at 4 °C, then gets lighter
It gets lighter the colder it becomes
It keeps getting denser right down to freezing
Its density does not change as it cools

items.explain: Unlike fresh water, seawater only gets denser as it cools, until it reaches its freezing point.

items.prompt: The Sun warms the ocean from above. Left to itself, what does this do to the layers of water?

options.label: Warm, lighter water floats on colder, denser water
Warm water sinks and drives strong deep currents
The whole ocean mixes evenly down to the seafloor
The surface water becomes saltier than the deep

items.explain: Heated surface water becomes less dense and floats above cooler, denser layers, which stratifies the ocean.

items.prompt: Sunlight alone leaves the ocean in stable layers. What lets heat-driven convection, and so deep currents, happen between those layers anyway?

options.label: Sunlight reaching all the way to the seafloor
Ships stirring the water as they cross the sea
Rain falling more heavily over the open ocean
Mixing of the layers by winds and tides

items.explain: Wind and tides mix the water layers, and this mixing is what enables convection between them and thus deep currents.

items.prompt: Suppose the Atlantic limb of this circulation, the AMOC, collapsed. What is predicted for many European countries?

options.label: Much hotter summers than today
Substantially lower temperatures
Far more tropical hurricanes
No noticeable change in weather

items.explain: A collapse of the AMOC would bring substantially lower temperatures to many European countries, while North America's east coast would see faster sea level rise.

items.prompt: Deep water formed in the North Atlantic fills the Arctic basin. Why can't it continue on into the Pacific Ocean?

options.label: Pacific water is too dense for it to enter
It freezes solid under the Arctic sea ice
The Bering Strait is too narrow and shallow
Strong winds push it back toward Europe

items.explain: The narrow shallows of the Bering Strait block it, so it flows slowly south into the deep Atlantic instead.
